title: Smith et al. (2007) True/False Quiz
instructions: Choose True or False, then examine how masculinity and aging shape the meanings of independence in each linked source segment. Interpret the participants' accounts as qualitative evidence, and distinguish the authors' practical proposals from demonstrated policy effects.

items.prompt: The paper defines older men's independence as a single masculine trait that always damages health.
items.explanation: The authors argue that independence has multiple meanings. It may be understood as health damaging in discussions of masculine self-reliance and help avoidance, but as health enhancing when associated with successful aging.

items.prompt: The definition of independence within hegemonic masculinity particularly privileges self-reliance and autonomy.
items.explanation: The article describes cultural expectations of independence, toughness, assertiveness, and other masculine traits. Within this construction, independence especially emphasizes self-reliance and autonomy; it is not presented as an inherent trait shared identically by all men.

items.prompt: In the article's discussion of successful aging, any reliance on other people automatically counts as unsuccessful aging.
items.explanation: The authors recognize different forms of dependency and levels of independence along a continuum of achievements. Reliance on others does not automatically imply failure to age successfully.

items.prompt: The full FAMAS cohort comprised 1,195 men aged 35–80, and 36 men were invited to the qualitative substudy using strata based on age and marital status.
items.explanation: The larger cohort was randomly drawn from a telephone directory in North-West Adelaide. The qualitative study recruited 36 men from that cohort; its interview accounts should not be treated as prevalence estimates for all older men.

items.prompt: According to the methods text, 22 of the 36 men in the qualitative substudy were over age 55, and 12 of those men were aged 65 or older.
items.explanation: These are the counts reported in the methods narrative. The authors primarily drew on these older participants' understandings, while the full qualitative sample also included younger men.

items.prompt: All in-depth interviews took place in health-service consulting rooms during the morning.
items.explanation: Most interviews took place at participants' homes in the afternoon or evening. On four occasions, a university interview room or a participant's workplace was used at the participant's request.

items.prompt: The age gap between the 25-year-old interviewer, JS, and participants, most of whom were aged 55 or older, was interpreted as an opportunity to elicit life-course accounts of health and masculinity.
items.explanation: Participants compared their younger years with the interviewer's stage of life. These reflections allowed JS to explore health and masculinity across their remembered experiences; they were not repeated observations across the participants' lifespans.

items.prompt: In the findings, independence as masculinity and independence as successful aging appeared as separate discourses that did not overlap.
items.explanation: The authors describe the two discourses as intertwined in participants' accounts. Independence meant both self-sufficiency as part of masculine identity and maintaining quality of life while aging.

items.prompt: Conrad's account of taking control of diabetes and Harry's account of remaining strong illustrate how control and toughness contributed to masculine meanings of independence.
items.explanation: Conrad emphasized controlling diabetes rather than being controlled by it. Harry emphasized staying strong and not always seeking help. The examples illustrate their meanings of independence, rather than demonstrating the health effects of those attitudes.

items.prompt: In Sam's, Ben's, and Arnold's accounts, partners' involvement or concern about burdening others appeared alongside self-reliant approaches to seeking help.
items.explanation: Sam and Ben described preferences for managing independently alongside their wives' views or involvement. Arnold chose not to call his lodger after a fall because he associated asking for help with being a burden.

items.prompt: The authors explained Max's refusal of nursing visits solely as innate stubbornness and disregarded his life experience.
items.explanation: Max connected his reluctance to a long history of looking after himself. The authors use this account to question a simple stereotype of stubborn older men and to examine the intersection of masculinity and aging.

items.prompt: In David's and Bob's accounts, independence was connected to quality of life through self-care, doing desired activities, and functioning physically and cognitively.
items.explanation: These middle-aged participants emphasized functioning and quality of life. David valued a full life and the ability to look after himself, while Bob emphasized physical and cognitive independence.

items.prompt: Roger's account was used to argue that maximizing lifespan took priority over his concerns about dependency and burdening others.
items.explanation: Roger worried about relying on others for feeding and personal care. The authors interpret his near-death experience as directing attention to quality of life, not simply the greatest possible longevity.

items.prompt: Arnold's use of an electric scooter illustrates how accepting an assistive device could reformulate independence and idealized masculinity.
items.explanation: The scooter enabled Arnold to reach local shops, the pharmacy, and his doctor on his own despite difficulty walking. In the authors' interpretation, redefining independence around daily functioning helped him sustain quality of life.

items.prompt: The authors' proposal for a less universal approach means applying the same policy to every subgroup of men.
items.explanation: The proposal calls for attention to the distinct concerns of particular groups, including older men, and for multiple perspectives on independence. It is an implication for practice and policy that warrants further examination, not an evaluated policy intervention.
